title: Cost-effectiveness of a smart pillbox intervention for adherence to oral HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis

paper_content.abstract: Despite proven oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) efficacy, adherence barriers among men who have sex with men (MSM) persist. Economic viability of digital adherence tools in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) requires validation. We assessed the 6-month within-trial cost-effectiveness of a digital intervention for real-time enhancement of oral PrEP adherence (DIRECT-PrEP) in China, from health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives. Costs were derived from hospital records, and effectiveness was evaluated using quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) and PrEP-adherence days (PADs). Among 442 participants (247 intervention, 195 standard care), incremental costs per QALY gained for the smart pillbox intervention were $19,575.93 (health system), $19,656.66 (multipayer), and $19,844.42 (societal)—all below the cost-effectiveness threshold of three times per capita gross domestic product ($31,200). Costs per PAD gained were $30.46–$30.86, achieving >95% probability of cost-effectiveness at willingness-to-pay thresholds of $47.50–$48.50 per PAD. Notably, the intervention demonstrated greater cost-effectiveness per QALY among participants stratified as more socially vulnerable ($16,259.77–$16,490.41) compared with those classified as less socially vulnerable ($23,514.83–$23,834.38). These results establish the smart-pillbox digital intervention as a cost-effective strategy for oral PrEP adherence within primary health care settings in LMICs, particularly when prioritizing more socially vulnerable populations, though long-term scalability requires further validation.
paper_content.introduction:
Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a cornerstone of HIV prevention for high-risk populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)1–3. Despite its efficacy, suboptimal adherence remains a critical barrier, diminishing protection at low adherence levels4 and increasing risks of HIV transmission and drug resistance5. MSM, as a key sexual minority group, experience heightened vulnerability due to Social Determinants of Health (SDH) spanning (1) conditions of daily life (e.g., behavioral patterns, social support) and (2) structural determinants (e.g., economic status, education)6. Consequently, investigating cost-effective interventions for more socially vulnerable MSM is crucial to advance health equity. The urgency of this issue has been further amplified by the COVID-19 pandemic and persistent health inequities have underscored the need for scalable digital solutions in LMICs, where structural constraints—limited healthcare infrastructure, funding shortages, and power supply instability—hinder conventional interventions7.

Achieving equity in HIV prevention requires an understanding of not only which interventions are effective, but also the mechanisms underlying their differential performance across SDH strata. SDH factors—such as socioeconomic status, education, and housing stability—directly influence PrEP persistence8. Furthermore, behavioral risk patterns among MSM9 (e.g., multiple sexual partners, engaging in condomless sex, and substance use) are shaped by these broader structural factors and collectively influence HIV risk and PrEP cost-effectiveness. Across diverse settings, suboptimal PrEP adherence among MSM remains a persistent challenge4, driven by stigma, socioeconomic marginalization, and discrimination10. These barriers are not unique to China but reflect structural determinants common to MSM globally. Moreover, high-risk MSM subgroups may demonstrate greater willingness to adopt PrEP11, yet structural barriers—such as limited psychosocial support or economic resources—often undermine adherence12, leading to variations in cost-effectiveness across different SDH strata.

UNAIDS estimates that adopting innovative technologies, efficiencies, and approaches could reduce annual HIV response costs by approximately US$7 billion13. Although digital adherence technologies [e.g., short message service (SMS) reminders, mobile apps] show promise, evidence of their effectiveness is heterogeneous. For instance, an interactive text-messaging intervention improved PrEP adherence among young MSM in Chicago14, yet SMS-based interventions failed among MSM in China and other vulnerable groups15–19. Moreover, whereas interactive messaging reduced sexual risk behaviors at incremental costs of $19.70–$131.60 per risk-reduction unit20,21, these approaches face scalability barriers: high start-up costs ($1021 per participant)22, declining engagement without reinforcement, and low suitability for populations with limited digital literacy7. Crucially, none adequately address the operational challenges of LMICs as effectively as electronic medication monitors (e.g., smart pillbox). Our randomized controlled trial (RCT) showed telemonitoring using electronic medication monitors increased oral PrEP adherence to 83.1% (21.0% net improvement over controls) over 6 months among Chinese MSM7. This efficacy stems from its user-centered design: real-time dose confirmation, minimal user input, and offline functionality align with people-centered strategies recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO)23.

Technologically, electronic medication monitors circumvent LMIC infrastructural barriers via low operational costs, accurate passive data collection, and seamless system integration. Unlike SMS or app-based platforms requiring continuous connectivity, these devices use durable, battery-powered hardware with predominantly one-time procurement costs24. Their automated monitoring eliminates reliance on self-reporting, thereby mitigating reporting inaccuracies common in LMICs25. Most importantly, their capacity to function independently of grid electricity or internet connectivity is critical in regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, where mobile network coverage gaps are about 50%26. Nevertheless, cost-effectiveness analyses specific to electronic medication monitors remain scarce. Existing economic evaluations of HIV-related mHealth focus disproportionately on SMS ($132–$314/participant) or video-based interventions ($1021/participant)21,22, overlooking electronic medication monitors’ potential for higher marginal returns at scale. For example, while two-way texting achieved cost savings for antiretroviral therapy retention in Malawi27, similar efficiencies were plausible for electronic medication monitors given their reusable infrastructure. China’s digital infrastructure has seen comparatively greater investment in recent years. However, contextual differences across LMICs may limit the generalizability of our findings to regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa. Evidence shows that LMIC health facilities often lack reliable internet, electricity, and digital infrastructure essential for implementing adherence technologies. For example, a survey of over 5000 facilities in eight LMICs reported very low digital infrastructure scores28. Similar assessments in South and Southeast Asia highlight persistent gaps in electricity, affordable connectivity, and policy support29. These disparities highlight the need for a systematic, human-centered, and contextually grounded approach to implementing digital HIV interventions in LMICs.

This study addresses two critical research gaps in digital health interventions for LMICs. First, it provides the economic evaluation of electronic medication monitors for oral PrEP adherence using LMIC-specific cost metrics, including cost per adherence-unit gained and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). Second, it adopts an equity-focused lens to assess the affordability of electronic medication monitors among more socially vulnerable and less socially vulnerable MSM by examining device durability and maintenance within LMIC resource constraints, thereby aligning with priorities for sustainable, device-led innovations.

Ultimately, by demonstrating the superiority of electronic medication monitors in cost per adherence-unit metrics and scalability within LMIC health systems, this study aims to inform global oral PrEP rollout strategies—advancing health equity through frugal, context-adapted medical devices.
paper_content.results:
Participant characteristics
Figure 1 presented the overall study design. Among the 516 participants who completed the baseline assessment, 247 were randomized to the smart pillbox intervention group and 195 to the control group (Supplementary Fig. S1). Baseline health utilities were comparable between groups, and no significant between-group differences in direct healthcare utilization costs were observed at baseline (Supplementary Table S1).

Cost components
Table 1 summarized the 6-month cost and health outcome profiles. From the health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives, the mean (standard deviation [SD]) cumulative total costs in the intervention group were $1826.77 (434.88), $1846.00 (434.71), and $1950.76 (434.82), respectively. The corresponding values for the control group were $1373.68 (585.34), $1390.19 (585.21), and $1488.52 (585.23). Healthcare utilization costs represented the predominant cost component for both groups (intervention: 78.37%; control: 78.69%; Supplementary Fig. S2), while intervention-related costs accounted for 8.08% of total intervention expenditures. Unadjusted intergroup cost differences were detailed in Table 2.

Direct costs: testing and intervention
Costs related to testing averaged $140.27 per participant. The mean intervention cost was $157.66 per participant (Table 1), of which $28.99 (18.39%) was allocated to the smart pillbox. Personnel expenditures constituted the majority of intervention costs at $121.32 per participant (76.95%). Costs associated with questionnaire administration and follow-up support were $2.88 per participant, representing 1.83% of total intervention expenditures (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Direct costs: healthcare utilization
The mean total healthcare utilization cost was significantly higher in the intervention group ($1528.85 [434.89]) compared with the control group ($1171.37 [585.35]; P<0.001, Table 2). Healthcare utilization represented the predominant non-intervention cost category across both groups (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Indirect costs
Venue and cohort maintenance costs were comparable between groups. However, the intervention group incurred slightly higher expenditures for food and transportation ($19.23 [1.37]) than the control group ($16.52 [1.38]). Time costs and lost productivity were also higher in the intervention group ($20.27 [1.63] vs. $13.83 [1.45]; Table 1).

Health effect
Table 2 showed significantly greater improvements in both QALYs and PrEP-adherence days (PADs) in the intervention group compared with the control group during the 6-month study period. The unadjusted mean difference was 32.72 (95% CI: 11.94–40.91) for PADs and 0.02 (95% CI: 0.01–0.02) for QALYs (intervention: 0.96 [SD 0.04] vs. control: 0.94 [SD 0.05]).

Cost-effectiveness
Table 3 presented the ICERs calculated from 6-month cost and effectiveness differentials using the SUR model. From the health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives, the smart pillbox intervention yielded ICERs per QALY gained of $19,575.93, $19,656.66, and $19,844.42, respectively. Cost-effectiveness acceptability curves demonstrated a 0.01–98.80% probability of intervention cost-effectiveness across willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds ranging from $10,400 to $31,200. For PADs, the intervention produced ICERs of $30.46, $30.58, and $30.86 per PAD gained from these respective perspectives. A WTP threshold between $47.50 and $48.50 per PAD was needed to achieve >95% probability of cost-effectiveness. Notably, at a WTP threshold equivalent to three times China’s per-capita GDP, the intervention demonstrated cost-effectiveness across all examined perspectives and outcomes compared with standard care. Results from the seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) model that was adjusted for baseline characteristics were presented in Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. S7–8.

The smart pillbox intervention was more cost-effective in the more socially vulnerable group, with ICERs ranging from $16,259.77 to $16,490.41 and a cost-effectiveness probability of 2.71–98.99%. In contrast, the less socially vulnerable group exhibited higher ICERs ($23,514.83–$23,834.38) and lower probability (0.08–82.15%). For PADs, the intervention showed ICERs of $26.73–$27.09 in the more socially vulnerable group but higher ICERs ($30.08–$30.47) in the less socially vulnerable group, both evaluated from the three perspectives (Table 4; Supplementary Fig. S3–6).

Sensitivity analyses
Figure 2 displayed the distribution of bootstrap-replicated net cost and QALY estimates on the cost-effectiveness plane. From the health system perspective, the probability of cost-effectiveness ranged from 0.02% (1/5000 replications) at a WTP threshold of 1× GDP per capita ($10,400) to 98.80% (4940/5000) at 3× GDP per capita ($31,200). Similarly, under the multipayer perspective, the probability ranged from 0.02% (1/5000) to 98.75% (4938/5000), while the societal perspective showed a range of 0.01% (1/5000) to 98.63% (4932/5000) across the same WTP thresholds. These findings were further supported by the CEAC illustrated in Fig. 3.

Robustness checks
Our results exhibited consistent robustness across all sensitivity analyses. First, reanalysis adjusted for baseline characteristics maintained significant improvements (PADs: 29.91 [95% CI: 15.68–44.14]); QALYs: 0.03 [95% CI: 0.02–0.03]), demonstrating consistent robustness (Supplementary Table S2). Second, ordinary least squares (OLS) analysis (baseline-adjusted) yielded comparable ICERs (QALYs: $18,897.47–$19,263.99; PADs: $30.71–$31.30; Supplementary Table S3, Figs. S9, 10). Third, generalized linear models (GLM) estimation of incremental costs revealed a 0.00–97.08% cost-effectiveness probability for QALYs at WTP thresholds of 1–3× GDP, with QALY ICERs of $21,121.95–$21,235.81 and PAD ICERs of $34.14–$34.32 across perspectives (Supplementary Table S4; Supplementary Figs. S11, 12). Fourth, treating overhead expenses as variable costs yielded an unadjusted societal ICER of $20,741.40, below three times GDP per capita (Supplementary Table S5). Fifth, using an alternative pooled HIV/AIDS utility value produced an unadjusted societal ICER of $19,793.40, also below this threshold (Supplementary Table S6). Sixth, when using an alternative WTP threshold (Supplementary Tables S7 and S8), the cost-effectiveness probability from the societal perspective among the more socially vulnerable group ranged from 9.30% to 98.57%. Finally, reanalysis using Truvada-specific costs (baseline-adjusted) showed that the probability of cost-effectiveness ranged from 5.64% to 99.94% (Supplementary Table S9). Critically, all analyses converged on a near-100% cost-effectiveness probability at the 3× GDP WTP threshold.
paper_content.methods:
The prospective interventional China Real-world Oral Intake of PrEP (CROPrEP) study evaluated the HIV prevention efficacy of TDF/FTC among MSM in four cities: Beijing, Shenzhen, Chongqing, and Shenyang48. Participants were stratified by baseline preference into daily or event-driven PrEP subgroups, or a non-PrEP group. Daily PrEP participants received one TDF/FTC tablet per day. The event-driven PrEP regimen involved administering two tablets 2–24 h before sexual intercourse, followed by single tablets 24 and 48 h after the initial dose. If additional sexual activity occurred within 48 h of the initial dose, participants transitioned to daily dosing until 48 h after the final sexual act. Subsequent sexual encounters triggered reinitiation of the event-driven regimen. Cross-over between daily and event-driven groups was permitted during follow-up.

The pragmatic RCT of the digital intervention for real-time enhancement of oral PrEP adherence (DIRECT-PrEP) study7 ran concurrently in the same cities. It was approved by the First Hospital of China Medical University Ethics Committee (No. 2019-253-3). Participants were stratified by PrEP regimen and randomized (1:1) to intervention or control groups using opaque sealed envelopes containing computer-generated random numbers. The trial protocol was previously published49. We adhered to Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting (CHEERS) 202250 (Supplementary Note 4).

Participants
CHWs and volunteers shared details of DIRECT-PrEP via WeChat to CROPrEP participants. After enrollment, MSM were randomized to intervention or control groups. Eligibility criteria included being biologically male, aged 18–65 years, engaging in anal sex with men, having at least one high-risk behavior in the past six months (condomless anal intercourse with males, ≥2 male partners, or any sexually transmitted infection diagnosis), confirmed HIV-1 negative status, participation in CROPrEP, ability to understand study protocols, and provision of written informed consent (Supplementary Protocol). Recruitment occurred between September 20, 2019, and November 27, 2020.

Five risk factors associated with higher social vulnerability were defined: ≤ high school education, monthly income <$580, relationship instability, having casual partners, and engaging in condomless anal intercourse with casual partners. Participants meeting two or more factors comprised the more socially vulnerable group, while others were classified as the less socially vulnerable group (Supplementary Note 1).

Intervention
This intervention leveraged an integrated technology-support model linking digital monitoring with clinical care to improve oral PrEP adherence. Key components included a multidisciplinary team, tailored participant engagement, structured follow-up, real-time communication, and supplementary resources to ensure sustained adherence and data integrity. Supplementary Fig. S13 illustrates the electronic medication monitoring device and its operation.

(1) Multidisciplinary team collaboration: The intervention involved a coordinated team of researchers, experienced physicians, and technical support personnel. Researchers facilitated proactive monitoring and participant contact, while physicians provided personalized adherence counseling and managed adverse events during follow-up visits. Technical experts ensured smart pillbox functionality. All roles were defined through standardized training before study initiation.

(2) Customized participant engagement protocols: Each participant received individualized support, including tailored instructional materials and demonstration videos for daily and event-driven PrEP use. Training content was refined iteratively based on feedback from pilot testing with researchers and users, emphasizing participant-centered engagement to promote self-management and adherence motivation.

(3) Structured monitoring and follow-up schedule: Participants underwent scheduled follow-ups at 3 and 6 months (±7 days), which included biological testing (e.g., HIV screening, HIV RNA pooling PCR, syphilis serology, HSV-2 antibody testing, routine blood and urine tests, liver and renal function tests, blood glucose and lipid profiles, and bone mineral density assessment) and online questionnaires assessing sociodemographic and behavioral factors. Continuous remote monitoring using the smart pillbox logged adherence data via cloud-based systems accessible through a WeChat Mini Program.

(4) Real-time alert and intervention mechanism: A multi-tiered reminder system was triggered by preset dosing schedules, incorporating multimodal alerts (sound, vibration, light, and WeChat push notifications) for missed doses. Missed-dose reminders escalated to repeated mobile notifications every 30 min (up to twice), followed by researcher alerts. Time-sensitive interventions were employed: doses missed before 22:00 were addressed immediately, while those after were handled by 10:00 the next day. Repeated pillbox openings without intake also triggered system alerts for researcher follow-up.

(5) Supplementary technical and operational resources: The intervention was supported by enhanced training materials, real-time technical assistance, and the provision of NB-IoT-enabled smart pillboxes with 600 mAh rechargeable batteries and automatic cloud logging. Post-study, devices were returned per a predefined protocol to ensure sustainability and data security. Supplementary resources such as customized instructional videos and a dedicated management platform facilitated seamless implementation.

Health effects
To quantify intervention effectiveness, two primary metrics were used: (1) health utility (QALYs) and (2) health effects (PADs) during follow-up.

QALYs provided a longitudinal measure of treatment effectiveness by integrating health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) states with time-in-state duration. Health utilities were derived from individual PrEP adherence levels. PrEP use as prescribed reduces sexual HIV acquisition risk by approximately 99% among MSM51; thus, perfect adherence was modeled as complete HIV protection. This framework allowed estimation of HIV incidence through adherence metrics. QALYs were calculated as a function of health utilities and estimated HIV incidence. To calculate PADs, PrEP medication adherence was assigned a value of 1 for perfect adherence and 0 for non-adherence. PrEP adherence was treated as a continuous variable, with imperfect adherence representing partial protection. PADs were calculated as (PrEP adherence) × (follow-up days) (Supplementary Note 2 for methodology).

Cost Components
Costs were categorized as testing, healthcare utilization, intervention, and indirect costs.

Direct costs: testing. Biological testing occurred at baseline, 3-month, and 6-month follow-ups. Total testing expenditure equaled the per-participant fixed cost multiplied by the eligible cohort size.

Direct costs: healthcare utilization. At the time of procurement, Truvada (TDF/FTC 300/200 mg; Gilead Sciences) cost $286.96 per 30-tablet bottle. Pill counts at baseline and follow-up visits determined total medication expenditure. Per-participant Truvada costs were calculated by distributing total expenditures across all randomized participants.

Direct costs: intervention. Smart pillbox costs included unit procurement, system development and maintenance (including software design), and charging expenses. Supplementary costs covered training materials, technical support, and NB-IoT-enabled smart pillboxes with rechargeable batteries and cloud auto-logging functionality. These expenditures also supported sustainability and data security through customized instructional videos and a dedicated management platform.

Labor costs included CHWs training and backend management (e.g., manual reminders for missed doses). Salaries were provided for two researchers and nurses conducting pill counts and adherence interventions. Additional costs covered travel, accommodation, and meals for training-related trips. One researcher responsible for pill counting and one nurse performing blood collection received part-time salaries for 15 months. Per-participant labor costs were calculated by dividing total expenditures across randomized participants. Two researchers implementing adherence interventions were compensated for 15 months, with costs allocated only to intervention group participants.

Questionnaire collection costs were based on the annual subscription fee ($579.57) for the Jinshuju data platform (https://jinshuju.net/home). Follow-up support expenses included communication costs covered by a 15-month phone plan at $28.84 per month. Per-participant questionnaire costs were calculated by dividing total expenditures across all randomized participants.

Indirect costs. venue, cohort maintenance, clinical visits, time, and lost productivity. Venue costs represented total expenditures across all four study sites. Cohort maintenance costs (a fixed fee) covered all participants at baseline and follow-up visits. Participant expenditures for food and transportation during clinical visits were extracted from survey data. Lost productivity was estimated by multiplying the number of clinical visits by the average daily wage, assuming a productivity loss of 2.5 h per visit for the intervention group and 2 h for the control group.

All costs were reported in 2020 U.S. dollars, using an exchange rate of 1 USD=6.9 CNY. Given the 6-month time horizon, no discounting was applied to costs or outcomes. Cost categories and analytical perspectives are presented in Supplementary Table S10.

Statistical analysis
We assessed efficacy using intent-to-treat analysis and trial-wide data from DIRECT-PrEP’s economic evaluation. The within-trial cost-effectiveness analysis compared the smart pillbox intervention with the control group across three perspectives: health system, multipayer, and societal. The healthcare perspective incorporated only direct medical expenditures. The multipayer perspective included health sector expenditures, intervention costs, and indirect costs associated with food and transportation. The societal perspective encompassed all additional indirect costs, including participants’ opportunity costs related to healthcare engagement and productivity losses due to illness. As recommended for public health economic evaluations, we prioritized the societal perspective because it provides an inclusive assessment of all costs affecting both beneficiaries and payers, thereby offering a comprehensive evaluation of societal impact (Supplementary Note 3, Supplementary Table S6)40.

We quantified cost-effectiveness using the ICER, calculated by dividing the difference in mean costs between the digital intervention and control groups by the corresponding difference in health outcomes (measured in both QALYs and PADs). The ICER represented the marginal cost required to achieve one additional unit of health benefit when implementing the smart pillbox intervention versus standard care.

Because a specific WTP threshold has not been established in China37, we adopted the cost-effectiveness threshold framework based on WHO-CHOICE and previous publications39–41, corresponding to 1–3 times China’s 2020 per capita gross domestic product (GDP). This yielded an evaluative range of $10,400–$31,200 per QALY gained, based on China’s economic parameters52. WTP thresholds were also estimated using a VSL conversion42, yielding a point estimate of 1.45 times GDP per capita, with a lower bound of about 1.16 times and an upper bound of about 2.90 times GDP per capita. Regarding PADs, in the lack of predefined WTP benchmarks, we derived the theoretical threshold required to attain a 95% probability of cost-effectiveness through probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

We applied the two-sided SUR model to specify cost and effectiveness regression equations, producing incremental cost and utility estimates. To address sampling uncertainty, we used a nonparametric bootstrap resampling approach with 5000 iterations. This method generated an empirical joint distribution of incremental costs and effects by repeatedly sampling with replacement from the original dataset53,54.

These bootstrap replications were used to construct 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The resulting uncertainty estimates were visualized on cost-effectiveness planes, providing a comprehensive depiction of the variability in our cost-effectiveness estimates. There were no missing data in this trial; all essential medical records were fully available and analytically adequate.

We subsequently developed cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) to estimate the probability that the intervention was cost-effective across a range of WTP thresholds for QALYs, analyzed from multiple economic perspectives. These CEACs provided policymakers with robust probabilistic evidence of cost-effectiveness, while accounting for key uncertainties inherent in economic evaluations39.

To evaluate the robustness of our primary findings, we conducted comprehensive sensitivity analyses. First, we accounted for residual confounding by controlling for baseline outcome measures (age, income, casual partner status, and PrEP regimen). Second, we reassessed cost-effectiveness using two-sided GLM as well as OLS regression models. Third, we reanalyzed cost-effectiveness after including healthcare expenditures attributable to Truvada. Fourth, we conducted a sensitivity analysis that disaggregated system costs into fixed and variable components, treating overhead expenses as variable. Finally, we performed a sensitivity analysis based on an alternative pooled utility value for HIV/AIDS.

All analyses were conducted using R version 4.4.1. Two-sided independent samples t-tests and two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests were applied for normally and non-normally distributed continuous variables, respectively. Estimates were reported with 95% confidence intervals, using two-tailed tests with α=0.05 (P<0.05). The trial was registered on the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR1900025604).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a smart pillbox–based electronic medication monitoring intervention (DIRECT-PrEP) to improve oral PrEP adherence among men who have sex with men in China, comparing it with standard care. Using trial data over six months, the analysis assessed costs (from health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives) and effectiveness (QALYs and PrEP-adherence days). Results showed that the intervention produced modest health gains (0.02 QALYs; 32.7 more adherence days) at incremental costs of about $400, yielding ICERs well below the willingness-to-pay threshold of three times China’s GDP per capita, particularly among socially vulnerable groups, supporting its potential as a cost-effective and equity-enhancing strategy in LMIC settings.
I have some comments below.
1. In Table 1, the definitions of the health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives are not entirely clear. Based on the cost breakdown, the health system perspective ($1826.77) is limited to direct medical expenditures—drug costs, testing, and intervention-related expenses (smart pillbox, labor, follow-up support). The multipayer perspective adds only patient-incurred food and transportation costs ($19.23), which implicitly assumes that patients receive PrEP services free of charge beyond these access-related expenses. The societal perspective goes further, incorporating not only time and productivity losses ($20.27) and a small learning cost for using the pillbox ($2.88), but also broader indirect system-level costs such as venue expenditures ($76.24) and cohort maintenance costs ($8.26). Together, these additions raise the cost to approximately $1950.76 but not exactly same (calculated as $1826.77 + $19.23 + $20.27 + $2.88 + $76.24 + $8.26 = $1953.65). It would be helpful to note what specific costs were included for each perspective in the Supplementary Note 3 beyond just the definitions.
2. The authors used Seemingly Unrelated Regression (SUR) as their primary analytic method, allowing adjustment for individual baseline covariates and accounting for correlation between costs and outcomes within the same patient. This regression-based ICER estimation produced incremental cost and effect estimates, and bootstrapping was applied to generate uncertainty distributions. However, authors report the system cost as a point estimate (e.g., software development costs divided by total participants); it is difficult to distinguish which costs are fixed versus variable across different population sizes. This matters because digital health interventions often have high fixed costs that diminish with scale, making cost-effectiveness highly sensitive to the size of the target population. Without clarity on cost structure, the generalizability of findings to other settings is limited. Accordingly, the analysis only accounts the uncertainty based on patients costs but not system side cost. Authors may address this as a limitation or consider additional sensitivity analyses that vary assumptions on system-side costs, in addition to patient-level variation, would better capture the potential economies of scale inherent in digital health delivery.
3. As the authors note, the observed adherence benefit was modest—0.02 QALYs and an increase in PrEP-adherence days (PADs: 221.47 vs 188.75). This QALY gain was derived through an adherence-based utility mapping, where adherence ≥95% was assigned a utility of 0.95–1.00, 80–94% mapped to 0.90–0.95, and <80% mapped to 0.81–0.90. Using linear interpolation, adherence was then linked to HIV incidence reduction, with the framework assuming complete protection at full adherence and applying a baseline incidence of 5.6 per 100 person-years (rounded to 0.06). While this approach offers a structured way to translate adherence into health outcomes, the justification for the chosen utility values is unclear—particularly the assumption that all adherence <80% falls within the relatively high 0.81–0.90 utility range. This may risk overestimating health benefits in low-adherence groups and warrants greater transparency or sensitivity analyses to test alternative mappings.
4. The sensitivity analyses primarily examined statistical methods (SUR, OLS, GLM) and cost perspectives (health system, multipayer, societal), but the differences across perspectives were minimal—multipayer added only patient food/transportation costs, while societal added modest productivity losses—resulting in only marginal changes in ICERs. More critical sources of uncertainty likely lie in system-level factors: how health systems adapt to implementing digital interventions in different settings, how cost-effectiveness changes with population scale given fixed costs, and whether the observed adherence difference (221.47 vs 188.75 PADs) can be sustained over the long term. Highlighting these structural uncertainties as limitations would strengthen the discussion, as they may have greater implications for generalizability.
5. The paper claims to incorporate “behavioral economic principles” by contrasting electronic medication monitors’ adherence-mediated prevention benefits with SMS interventions’ focus on risk-behavior modification. However, the trial design and economic model evaluate only adherence outcomes (PADs, QALYs) and do not measure or compare downstream behavioral risk changes such as sexual risk compensation or reductions in risky behaviors. As a result, the use of “behavioral economics” feels more rhetorical than methodological: the study does not empirically test behavioral constructs but rather frames adherence versus behavior-modification strategies as distinct economic logics.
(Remarks on code availability)
The code runs three regression-based CEA methods (SUR, OLS, GLM) with bootstrapping, estimates incremental cost and effect, calculates ICERs, and visualizes uncertainty with cost-effectiveness planes and CEACs.
Not directly runnable as-is. The code has placeholders (xxx) for covariates and a hard-coded local path (C:/Users/xxx/xxx.csv). There’s no example dataset, no schema for required columns (e.g., class, cost_m0, effectiveness_m0, units), and no package version pinning.
No README / run instructions are shown in the snippet (installation steps, data dictionary, session info, or a one-command pipeline).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Thank you for the opportunity to review this manuscript. This cost-effective analysis of an intervention to improve PrEP adherence is novel and will be of interest to readers. It is mostly well written but requires some editing for readability which can hopefully be improved after copyediting. I have only two main thoughts for the authors to consider:
Six months doesn’t seem long enough, shouldn’t you extrapolate to consider health outcomes and downstream savings?
Personnel costs are a major driver of intervention costs. This raises questions about scalability. Discussion should better distinguish between trial-specific research costs vs. routine implementation costs.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The research investigates a critical economic analysis related to oral PrEP adherence in the MSM population. Focusing on equity is of utmost importance, considering that those in lower socioeconomic strata are disproportionately impacted by HIV. The methodology is generally sound and appropriately applied, however, certain critical areas warrant attention, and the paper does not meet the rigorous standards for Nature Communications.
Major comments:
1. The trial is China-specific, and while often considered a LMIC in public health research, the health system differences may limit generalizability to regions like Sub-Saharan Africa. And especially since the digitial infrastructure differ significantly from many LMICs. This limitation should be acknowledged consistently throughout the manuscript, not just in the discussion.
2. The use of Seemingly Unrelated Regression (SUR) and bootstrap simulations is unconventional for health economic modeling. While SUR can account for correlated outcomes, it is not standard for cost-effectiveness analysis, which typically relies on decision-analytic models. Can the authors justify why SUR was chosen over more established modelling methods? Also explain its limitations compared to more dynamic or long-term modelling.
3. The conclusion that "intervention complexity" is positively associated with equitable health coverage is not directly supported by the literature review presented in the “Comparison with existing Literature” paragraph, especially since the authors are trying to make this claim by comparing across different settings, time horizons, years. However, this interpretation oversimplifies the literature and possibly conflates methodological differences with causal relationships. The authors should either reframe this as a hypothesis or provide empirical justification.
4. While the study references willingness to pay (WTP) thresholds to interpret cost-effectiveness, it does not discuss their origin, appropriateness, or limitation, especially in the context of equity. WTP thresholds are often arbitrary and often fail to reflect societal values or budget constraints in LMICs. The authors could strengthen their analysis by discussing alternative approaches (e.g., opportunity cost-based thresholds, equity-weighted thresholds).
Minor comments:
1. The study focuses on MSM in China but does not engage with broader literature on PrEP adherence among MSM globally. There is little discussion of behavioral, structural, or psychosocial factors that influence adherence, nor of intersectional vulnerabilities such as stigma, income, or housing. This limits the depth of the equity framing and the relevance of findings to other MSM populations.
2. Personnel costs are the main driver of the intervention budget (>76%). This raises questions about scalability and whether similar staffing models are feasible in other LMICs.
3. PADs are a useful intermediate metric, but their translation into long-term HIV prevention outcomes could be better contextualized. The study uses perfect adherence as a binary threshold, yet imperfect adherence still conveys partial protection and this is not accounted for in the modelling. A more nuanced approach is needed. Perhaps modeling adherence as a gradient would better reflect real-world effectiveness.
4. The reported probability range for cost-effectiveness, eg. 2.71% to 98.99%, is extremely broad, limiting its practicality. This suggests high sensitivity to input assumptions or model structure. The authors should clarify which scenarios drive the lower bound and consider presenting threshold analyses to guide decision-makers more effectively.
5. The stratification by SDH is descriptive and limited to cost-effectiveness outcomes. The study does not explore underlying mechanisms or contextual factors that explain why cost-effectiveness differs by SDH strata—thus falling short of a deeper equity analysis.
6. The claim that smart pillboxes "critically extend" existing evidence is not fully substantiated. The comparison of incremental costs ($19,844 vs. $24,705 for SMS) lacks context—are these figures derived from comparable methodologies, time horizons, and costing perspectives?
7. The critique of other digital tools (SMS, apps, hybrid models) is broad and somewhat selective. For example, citing $1021/user for a U.S. MSM app without adjusting for context or scale may unfairly skew the comparison.
8. Granted that English might not be the first language for the authors, however, spelling errors could be avoided by using a spell checker, e.g. hightened=heightened; siginificant=significant; coverd=covered; trail-wide=trial-wide; to name a few.

The authors have addressed the initial concerns by acknowledging key limitations and adding relevant sensitivity analyses. However, the analytic design still does not sufficiently engage with the major system-level drivers—particularly the role of fixed versus variable program costs. Instead, it focuses primarily on relatively small variations in patient-level costs, which yield very similar results across perspectives. This narrow focus constrains the overall significance and policy relevance of the findings. Several tables therefore present only marginal differences, offering limited additional insight despite the application of innovative and comprehensive statistical methods.
That said, the study provides detailed program information and demonstrates a rigorous analytic process using rich data. These contributions may support future work that addresses more consequential system-level questions and explores scenarios where meaningful differences are more likely to emerge.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Despite proven oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) efficacy, adherence barriers among men who have sex with men (MSM) persist. Economic viability of digital adherence tools in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) requires validation. We assessed the 6-month within-trial cost-effectiveness of a digital intervention for real-time enhancement of oral PrEP adherence (DIRECT-PrEP) in China, from health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives. Costs were derived from hospital records, and effectiveness was evaluated using quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) and PrEP-adherence days (PADs). Among 442 participants (247 intervention, 195 standard care), incremental costs per QALY gained for the smart pillbox intervention were $19,575.93 (health system), $19,656.66 (multipayer), and $19,844.42 (societal)—all below the cost-effectiveness threshold of three times per capita gross domestic product ($31,200). Costs per PAD gained were $30.46–$30.86, achieving >95% probability of cost-effectiveness at willingness-to-pay thresholds of $47.50–$48.50 per PAD. Notably, the intervention demonstrated greater cost-effectiveness per QALY among participants stratified as more socially vulnerable ($16,259.77–$16,490.41) compared with those classified as less socially vulnerable ($23,514.83–$23,834.38). These results establish the smart-pillbox digital intervention as a cost-effective strategy for oral PrEP adherence within primary health care settings in LMICs, particularly when prioritizing more socially vulnerable populations, though long-term scalability requires further validation.

---

## Introduction

Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a cornerstone of HIV prevention for high-risk populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)1–3. Despite its efficacy, suboptimal adherence remains a critical barrier, diminishing protection at low adherence levels4 and increasing risks of HIV transmission and drug resistance5. MSM, as a key sexual minority group, experience heightened vulnerability due to Social Determinants of Health (SDH) spanning (1) conditions of daily life (e.g., behavioral patterns, social support) and (2) structural determinants (e.g., economic status, education)6. Consequently, investigating cost-effective interventions for more socially vulnerable MSM is crucial to advance health equity. The urgency of this issue has been further amplified by the COVID-19 pandemic and persistent health inequities have underscored the need for scalable digital solutions in LMICs, where structural constraints—limited healthcare infrastructure, funding shortages, and power supply instability—hinder conventional interventions7.

Achieving equity in HIV prevention requires an understanding of not only which interventions are effective, but also the mechanisms underlying their differential performance across SDH strata. SDH factors—such as socioeconomic status, education, and housing stability—directly influence PrEP persistence8. Furthermore, behavioral risk patterns among MSM9 (e.g., multiple sexual partners, engaging in condomless sex, and substance use) are shaped by these broader structural factors and collectively influence HIV risk and PrEP cost-effectiveness. Across diverse settings, suboptimal PrEP adherence among MSM remains a persistent challenge4, driven by stigma, socioeconomic marginalization, and discrimination10. These barriers are not unique to China but reflect structural determinants common to MSM globally. Moreover, high-risk MSM subgroups may demonstrate greater willingness to adopt PrEP11, yet structural barriers—such as limited psychosocial support or economic resources—often undermine adherence12, leading to variations in cost-effectiveness across different SDH strata.

UNAIDS estimates that adopting innovative technologies, efficiencies, and approaches could reduce annual HIV response costs by approximately US$7 billion13. Although digital adherence technologies [e.g., short message service (SMS) reminders, mobile apps] show promise, evidence of their effectiveness is heterogeneous. For instance, an interactive text-messaging intervention improved PrEP adherence among young MSM in Chicago14, yet SMS-based interventions failed among MSM in China and other vulnerable groups15–19. Moreover, whereas interactive messaging reduced sexual risk behaviors at incremental costs of $19.70–$131.60 per risk-reduction unit20,21, these approaches face scalability barriers: high start-up costs ($1021 per participant)22, declining engagement without reinforcement, and low suitability for populations with limited digital literacy7. Crucially, none adequately address the operational challenges of LMICs as effectively as electronic medication monitors (e.g., smart pillbox). Our randomized controlled trial (RCT) showed telemonitoring using electronic medication monitors increased oral PrEP adherence to 83.1% (21.0% net improvement over controls) over 6 months among Chinese MSM7. This efficacy stems from its user-centered design: real-time dose confirmation, minimal user input, and offline functionality align with people-centered strategies recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO)23.

Technologically, electronic medication monitors circumvent LMIC infrastructural barriers via low operational costs, accurate passive data collection, and seamless system integration. Unlike SMS or app-based platforms requiring continuous connectivity, these devices use durable, battery-powered hardware with predominantly one-time procurement costs24. Their automated monitoring eliminates reliance on self-reporting, thereby mitigating reporting inaccuracies common in LMICs25. Most importantly, their capacity to function independently of grid electricity or internet connectivity is critical in regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, where mobile network coverage gaps are about 50%26. Nevertheless, cost-effectiveness analyses specific to electronic medication monitors remain scarce. Existing economic evaluations of HIV-related mHealth focus disproportionately on SMS ($132–$314/participant) or video-based interventions ($1021/participant)21,22, overlooking electronic medication monitors’ potential for higher marginal returns at scale. For example, while two-way texting achieved cost savings for antiretroviral therapy retention in Malawi27, similar efficiencies were plausible for electronic medication monitors given their reusable infrastructure. China’s digital infrastructure has seen comparatively greater investment in recent years. However, contextual differences across LMICs may limit the generalizability of our findings to regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa. Evidence shows that LMIC health facilities often lack reliable internet, electricity, and digital infrastructure essential for implementing adherence technologies. For example, a survey of over 5000 facilities in eight LMICs reported very low digital infrastructure scores28. Similar assessments in South and Southeast Asia highlight persistent gaps in electricity, affordable connectivity, and policy support29. These disparities highlight the need for a systematic, human-centered, and contextually grounded approach to implementing digital HIV interventions in LMICs.

This study addresses two critical research gaps in digital health interventions for LMICs. First, it provides the economic evaluation of electronic medication monitors for oral PrEP adherence using LMIC-specific cost metrics, including cost per adherence-unit gained and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). Second, it adopts an equity-focused lens to assess the affordability of electronic medication monitors among more socially vulnerable and less socially vulnerable MSM by examining device durability and maintenance within LMIC resource constraints, thereby aligning with priorities for sustainable, device-led innovations.

Ultimately, by demonstrating the superiority of electronic medication monitors in cost per adherence-unit metrics and scalability within LMIC health systems, this study aims to inform global oral PrEP rollout strategies—advancing health equity through frugal, context-adapted medical devices.

---

## Results

Participant characteristics
Figure 1 presented the overall study design. Among the 516 participants who completed the baseline assessment, 247 were randomized to the smart pillbox intervention group and 195 to the control group (Supplementary Fig. S1). Baseline health utilities were comparable between groups, and no significant between-group differences in direct healthcare utilization costs were observed at baseline (Supplementary Table S1).

Cost components
Table 1 summarized the 6-month cost and health outcome profiles. From the health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives, the mean (standard deviation [SD]) cumulative total costs in the intervention group were $1826.77 (434.88), $1846.00 (434.71), and $1950.76 (434.82), respectively. The corresponding values for the control group were $1373.68 (585.34), $1390.19 (585.21), and $1488.52 (585.23). Healthcare utilization costs represented the predominant cost component for both groups (intervention: 78.37%; control: 78.69%; Supplementary Fig. S2), while intervention-related costs accounted for 8.08% of total intervention expenditures. Unadjusted intergroup cost differences were detailed in Table 2.

Direct costs: testing and intervention
Costs related to testing averaged $140.27 per participant. The mean intervention cost was $157.66 per participant (Table 1), of which $28.99 (18.39%) was allocated to the smart pillbox. Personnel expenditures constituted the majority of intervention costs at $121.32 per participant (76.95%). Costs associated with questionnaire administration and follow-up support were $2.88 per participant, representing 1.83% of total intervention expenditures (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Direct costs: healthcare utilization
The mean total healthcare utilization cost was significantly higher in the intervention group ($1528.85 [434.89]) compared with the control group ($1171.37 [585.35]; P<0.001, Table 2). Healthcare utilization represented the predominant non-intervention cost category across both groups (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Indirect costs
Venue and cohort maintenance costs were comparable between groups. However, the intervention group incurred slightly higher expenditures for food and transportation ($19.23 [1.37]) than the control group ($16.52 [1.38]). Time costs and lost productivity were also higher in the intervention group ($20.27 [1.63] vs. $13.83 [1.45]; Table 1).

Health effect
Table 2 showed significantly greater improvements in both QALYs and PrEP-adherence days (PADs) in the intervention group compared with the control group during the 6-month study period. The unadjusted mean difference was 32.72 (95% CI: 11.94–40.91) for PADs and 0.02 (95% CI: 0.01–0.02) for QALYs (intervention: 0.96 [SD 0.04] vs. control: 0.94 [SD 0.05]).

Cost-effectiveness
Table 3 presented the ICERs calculated from 6-month cost and effectiveness differentials using the SUR model. From the health system, multipayer, and societal perspectives, the smart pillbox intervention yielded ICERs per QALY gained of $19,575.93, $19,656.66, and $19,844.42, respectively. Cost-effectiveness acceptability curves demonstrated a 0.01–98.80% probability of intervention cost-effectiveness across willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds ranging from $10,400 to $31,200. For PADs, the intervention produced ICERs of $30.46, $30.58, and $30.86 per PAD gained from these respective perspectives. A WTP threshold between $47.50 and $48.50 per PAD was needed to achieve >95% probability of cost-effectiveness. Notably, at a WTP threshold equivalent to three times China’s per-capita GDP, the intervention demonstrated cost-effectiveness across all examined perspectives and outcomes compared with standard care. Results from the seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) model that was adjusted for baseline characteristics were presented in Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. S7–8.

The smart pillbox intervention was more cost-effective in the more socially vulnerable group, with ICERs ranging from $16,259.77 to $16,490.41 and a cost-effectiveness probability of 2.71–98.99%. In contrast, the less socially vulnerable group exhibited higher ICERs ($23,514.83–$23,834.38) and lower probability (0.08–82.15%). For PADs, the intervention showed ICERs of $26.73–$27.09 in the more socially vulnerable group but higher ICERs ($30.08–$30.47) in the less socially vulnerable group, both evaluated from the three perspectives (Table 4; Supplementary Fig. S3–6).

Sensitivity analyses
Figure 2 displayed the distribution of bootstrap-replicated net cost and QALY estimates on the cost-effectiveness plane. From the health system perspective, the probability of cost-effectiveness ranged from 0.02% (1/5000 replications) at a WTP threshold of 1× GDP per capita ($10,400) to 98.80% (4940/5000) at 3× GDP per capita ($31,200). Similarly, under the multipayer perspective, the probability ranged from 0.02% (1/5000) to 98.75% (4938/5000), while the societal perspective showed a range of 0.01% (1/5000) to 98.63% (4932/5000) across the same WTP thresholds. These findings were further supported by the CEAC illustrated in Fig. 3.

Robustness checks
Our results exhibited consistent robustness across all sensitivity analyses. First, reanalysis adjusted for baseline characteristics maintained significant improvements (PADs: 29.91 [95% CI: 15.68–44.14]); QALYs: 0.03 [95% CI: 0.02–0.03]), demonstrating consistent robustness (Supplementary Table S2). Second, ordinary least squares (OLS) analysis (baseline-adjusted) yielded comparable ICERs (QALYs: $18,897.47–$19,263.99; PADs: $30.71–$31.30; Supplementary Table S3, Figs. S9, 10). Third, generalized linear models (GLM) estimation of incremental costs revealed a 0.00–97.08% cost-effectiveness probability for QALYs at WTP thresholds of 1–3× GDP, with QALY ICERs of $21,121.95–$21,235.81 and PAD ICERs of $34.14–$34.32 across perspectives (Supplementary Table S4; Supplementary Figs. S11, 12). Fourth, treating overhead expenses as variable costs yielded an unadjusted societal ICER of $20,741.40, below three times GDP per capita (Supplementary Table S5). Fifth, using an alternative pooled HIV/AIDS utility value produced an unadjusted societal ICER of $19,793.40, also below this threshold (Supplementary Table S6). Sixth, when using an alternative WTP threshold (Supplementary Tables S7 and S8), the cost-effectiveness probability from the societal perspective among the more socially vulnerable group ranged from 9.30% to 98.57%. Finally, reanalysis using Truvada-specific costs (baseline-adjusted) showed that the probability of cost-effectiveness ranged from 5.64% to 99.94% (Supplementary Table S9). Critically, all analyses converged on a near-100% cost-effectiveness probability at the 3× GDP WTP threshold.

---

## Methods

The prospective interventional China Real-world Oral Intake of PrEP (CROPrEP) study evaluated the HIV prevention efficacy of TDF/FTC among MSM in four cities: Beijing, Shenzhen, Chongqing, and Shenyang48. Participants were stratified by baseline preference into daily or event-driven PrEP subgroups, or a non-PrEP group. Daily PrEP participants received one TDF/FTC tablet per day. The event-driven PrEP regimen involved administering two tablets 2–24 h before sexual intercourse, followed by single tablets 24 and 48 h after the initial dose. If additional sexual activity occurred within 48 h of the initial dose, participants transitioned to daily dosing until 48 h after the final sexual act. Subsequent sexual encounters triggered reinitiation of the event-driven regimen. Cross-over between daily and event-driven groups was permitted during follow-up.

The pragmatic RCT of the digital intervention for real-time enhancement of oral PrEP adherence (DIRECT-PrEP) study7 ran concurrently in the same cities. It was approved by the First Hospital of China Medical University Ethics Committee (No. 2019-253-3). Participants were stratified by PrEP regimen and randomized (1:1) to intervention or control groups using opaque sealed envelopes containing computer-generated random numbers. The trial protocol was previously published49. We adhered to Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting (CHEERS) 202250 (Supplementary Note 4).

Participants
CHWs and volunteers shared details of DIRECT-PrEP via WeChat to CROPrEP participants. After enrollment, MSM were randomized to intervention or control groups. Eligibility criteria included being biologically male, aged 18–65 years, engaging in anal sex with men, having at least one high-risk behavior in the past six months (condomless anal intercourse with males, ≥2 male partners, or any sexually transmitted infection diagnosis), confirmed HIV-1 negative status, participation in CROPrEP, ability to understand study protocols, and provision of written informed consent (Supplementary Protocol). Recruitment occurred between September 20, 2019, and November 27, 2020.

Five risk factors associated with higher social vulnerability were defined: ≤ high school education, monthly income <$580, relationship instability, having casual partners, and engaging in condomless anal intercourse with casual partners. Participants meeting two or more factors comprised the more socially vulnerable group, while others were classified as the less socially vulnerable group (Supplementary Note 1).

Intervention
This intervention leveraged an integrated technology-support model linking digital monitoring with clinical care to improve oral PrEP adherence. Key components included a multidisciplinary team, tailored participant engagement, structured follow-up, real-time communication, and supplementary resources to ensure sustained adherence and data integrity. Supplementary Fig. S13 illustrates the electronic medication monitoring device and its operation.

(1) Multidisciplinary team collaboration: The intervention involved a coordinated team of researchers, experienced physicians, and technical support personnel. Researchers facilitated proactive monitoring and participant contact, while physicians provided personalized adherence counseling and managed adverse events during follow-up visits. Technical experts ensured smart pillbox functionality. All roles were defined through standardized training before study initiation.

(2) Customized participant engagement protocols: Each participant received individualized support, including tailored instructional materials and demonstration videos for daily and event-driven PrEP use. Training content was refined iteratively based on feedback from pilot testing with researchers and users, emphasizing participant-centered engagement to promote self-management and adherence motivation.

(3) Structured monitoring and follow-up schedule: Participants underwent scheduled follow-ups at 3 and 6 months (±7 days), which included biological testing (e.g., HIV screening, HIV RNA pooling PCR, syphilis serology, HSV-2 antibody testing, routine blood and urine tests, liver and renal function tests, blood glucose and lipid profiles, and bone mineral density assessment) and online questionnaires assessing sociodemographic and behavioral factors. Continuous remote monitoring using the smart pillbox logged adherence data via cloud-based systems accessible through a WeChat Mini Program.

(4) Real-time alert and intervention mechanism: A multi-tiered reminder system was triggered by preset dosing schedules, incorporating multimodal alerts (sound, vibration, light, and WeChat push notifications) for missed doses. Missed-dose reminders escalated to repeated mobile notifications every 30 min (up to twice), followed by researcher alerts. Time-sensitive interventions were employed: doses missed before 22:00 were addressed immediately, while those after were handled by 10:00 the next day. Repeated pillbox openings without intake also triggered system alerts for researcher follow-up.

(5) Supplementary technical and operational resources: The intervention was supported by enhanced training materials, real-time technical assistance, and the provision of NB-IoT-enabled smart pillboxes with 600 mAh rechargeable batteries and automatic cloud logging. Post-study, devices were returned per a predefined protocol to ensure sustainability and data security. Supplementary resources such as customized instructional videos and a dedicated management platform facilitated seamless implementation.

Health effects
To quantify intervention effectiveness, two primary metrics were used: (1) health utility (QALYs) and (2) health effects (PADs) during follow-up.

QALYs provided a longitudinal measure of treatment effectiveness by integrating health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) states with time-in-state duration. Health utilities were derived from individual PrEP adherence levels. PrEP use as prescribed reduces sexual HIV acquisition risk by approximately 99% among MSM51; thus, perfect adherence was modeled as complete HIV protection. This framework allowed estimation of HIV incidence through adherence metrics. QALYs were calculated as a function of health utilities and estimated HIV incidence. To calculate PADs, PrEP medication adherence was assigned a value of 1 for perfect adherence and 0 for non-adherence. PrEP adherence was treated as a continuous variable, with imperfect adherence representing partial protection. PADs were calculated as (PrEP adherence) × (follow-up days) (Supplementary Note 2 for methodology).

Cost Components
Costs were categorized as testing, healthcare utilization, intervention, and indirect costs.

Direct costs: testing. Biological testing occurred at baseline, 3-month, and 6-month follow-ups. Total testing expenditure equaled the per-participant fixed cost multiplied by the eligible cohort size.

Direct costs: healthcare utilization. At the time of procurement, Truvada (TDF/FTC 300/200 mg; Gilead Sciences) cost $286.96 per 30-tablet bottle. Pill counts at baseline and follow-up visits determined total medication expenditure. Per-participant Truvada costs were calculated by distributing total expenditures across all randomized participants.

Direct costs: intervention. Smart pillbox costs included unit procurement, system development and maintenance (including software design), and charging expenses. Supplementary costs covered training materials, technical support, and NB-IoT-enabled smart pillboxes with rechargeable batteries and cloud auto-logging functionality. These expenditures also supported sustainability and data security through customized instructional videos and a dedicated management platform.

Labor costs included CHWs training and backend management (e.g., manual reminders for missed doses). Salaries were provided for two researchers and nurses conducting pill counts and adherence interventions. Additional costs covered travel, accommodation, and meals for training-related trips. One researcher responsible for pill counting and one nurse performing blood collection received part-time salaries for 15 months. Per-participant labor costs were calculated by dividing total expenditures across randomized participants. Two researchers implementing adherence interventions were compensated for 15 months, with costs allocated only to intervention group participants.

Questionnaire collection costs were based on the annual subscription fee ($579.57) for the Jinshuju data platform (https://jinshuju.net/home). Follow-up support expenses included communication costs covered by a 15-month phone plan at $28.84 per month. Per-participant questionnaire costs were calculated by dividing total expenditures across all randomized participants.

Indirect costs. venue, cohort maintenance, clinical visits, time, and lost productivity. Venue costs represented total expenditures across all four study sites. Cohort maintenance costs (a fixed fee) covered all participants at baseline and follow-up visits. Participant expenditures for food and transportation during clinical visits were extracted from survey data. Lost productivity was estimated by multiplying the number of clinical visits by the average daily wage, assuming a productivity loss of 2.5 h per visit for the intervention group and 2 h for the control group.

All costs were reported in 2020 U.S. dollars, using an exchange rate of 1 USD=6.9 CNY. Given the 6-month time horizon, no discounting was applied to costs or outcomes. Cost categories and analytical perspectives are presented in Supplementary Table S10.

Statistical analysis
We assessed efficacy using intent-to-treat analysis and trial-wide data from DIRECT-PrEP’s economic evaluation. The within-trial cost-effectiveness analysis compared the smart pillbox intervention with the control group across three perspectives: health system, multipayer, and societal. The healthcare perspective incorporated only direct medical expenditures. The multipayer perspective included health sector expenditures, intervention costs, and indirect costs associated with food and transportation. The societal perspective encompassed all additional indirect costs, including participants’ opportunity costs related to healthcare engagement and productivity losses due to illness. As recommended for public health economic evaluations, we prioritized the societal perspective because it provides an inclusive assessment of all costs affecting both beneficiaries and payers, thereby offering a comprehensive evaluation of societal impact (Supplementary Note 3, Supplementary Table S6)40.

We quantified cost-effectiveness using the ICER, calculated by dividing the difference in mean costs between the digital intervention and control groups by the corresponding difference in health outcomes (measured in both QALYs and PADs). The ICER represented the marginal cost required to achieve one additional unit of health benefit when implementing the smart pillbox intervention versus standard care.

Because a specific WTP threshold has not been established in China37, we adopted the cost-effectiveness threshold framework based on WHO-CHOICE and previous publications39–41, corresponding to 1–3 times China’s 2020 per capita gross domestic product (GDP). This yielded an evaluative range of $10,400–$31,200 per QALY gained, based on China’s economic parameters52. WTP thresholds were also estimated using a VSL conversion42, yielding a point estimate of 1.45 times GDP per capita, with a lower bound of about 1.16 times and an upper bound of about 2.90 times GDP per capita. Regarding PADs, in the lack of predefined WTP benchmarks, we derived the theoretical threshold required to attain a 95% probability of cost-effectiveness through probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

We applied the two-sided SUR model to specify cost and effectiveness regression equations, producing incremental cost and utility estimates. To address sampling uncertainty, we used a nonparametric bootstrap resampling approach with 5000 iterations. This method generated an empirical joint distribution of incremental costs and effects by repeatedly sampling with replacement from the original dataset53,54.

These bootstrap replications were used to construct 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The resulting uncertainty estimates were visualized on cost-effectiveness planes, providing a comprehensive depiction of the variability in our cost-effectiveness estimates. There were no missing data in this trial; all essential medical records were fully available and analytically adequate.

We subsequently developed cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) to estimate the probability that the intervention was cost-effective across a range of WTP thresholds for QALYs, analyzed from multiple economic perspectives. These CEACs provided policymakers with robust probabilistic evidence of cost-effectiveness, while accounting for key uncertainties inherent in economic evaluations39.

To evaluate the robustness of our primary findings, we conducted comprehensive sensitivity analyses. First, we accounted for residual confounding by controlling for baseline outcome measures (age, income, casual partner status, and PrEP regimen). Second, we reassessed cost-effectiveness using two-sided GLM as well as OLS regression models. Third, we reanalyzed cost-effectiveness after including healthcare expenditures attributable to Truvada. Fourth, we conducted a sensitivity analysis that disaggregated system costs into fixed and variable components, treating overhead expenses as variable. Finally, we performed a sensitivity analysis based on an alternative pooled utility value for HIV/AIDS.

All analyses were conducted using R version 4.4.1. Two-sided independent samples t-tests and two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests were applied for normally and non-normally distributed continuous variables, respectively. Estimates were reported with 95% confidence intervals, using two-tailed tests with α=0.05 (P<0.05). The trial was registered on the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR1900025604).
